22:["$","p",null,{"children":"A path is a claim about a world that no longer exists. It was computed from a map, and the map was\nrecorded before the chair moved, before somebody left a box in the corridor, before the person\nwalking toward Rusty decided which side to pass on."}]
23:["$","p",null,{"children":"A tracking controller cannot fix this, because it is not being asked to. Give it a path and it will\nminimize the distance to that path, which is precisely the wrong objective when the path goes\nthrough a chair. Re-running the global planner instead is honest but expensive: at twenty hertz,\nwith a planner that takes a hundred milliseconds and returns a structurally different path each\ntime, Rusty would spend his life twitching between homotopy classes."}]
24:["$","p",null,{"children":["The receding-horizon answer is narrower and cheaper. Do not re-plan the route. Re-solve, every\ncycle, a ",["$","em",null,{"children":"short"}]," optimal control problem — two seconds, not two minutes — that already knows about\nthe chair, and execute one step of its answer."]}]

27:["$","p",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"Nothing here is optimized in the usual sense."}]," There is no gradient, no line search, no\nconvexity. Two hundred perturbed plans are simulated forward, each is assigned a number, and the\nnext plan is a weighted average. That is the entire algorithm, and it is the reason the obstacle\ncost is allowed to be a hard ",["$","code",null,{"children":"if"}]," statement over an occupancy grid."]}]
28:["$","p",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"The purple plan is not one of the orange rollouts."}]," It is their weighted mean, and it is visibly\nsmoother than any of them — the signature of an ",["$","em",null,{"children":"expectation"}]," rather than a selection. When the\ntemperature is pushed toward zero this stops being true, and the plan snaps onto whichever single\nrollout got lucky. Watch the effective sample size collapse toward 1 when you do it."]}]

2c:["$","p",null,{"children":["Before the path-integral machinery, the classical baseline — and it is a good one, still shipping in\nproduction stacks thirty years later. Fox, Burgard and Thrun's ",["$","strong",null,{"children":"Dynamic Window Approach"}]," starts\nfrom a physical observation: a differential-drive robot cannot execute an arbitrary curve. Over one\nshort control period it executes an arc, and which arcs are available is decided by its acceleration\nlimits. So do not search over paths. Search over the ",["$","em",null,{"children":"velocities"}]," reachable in the next period."]}]
2d:["$","p",null,{"children":"That search space is two-dimensional and tiny, which is why DWA ran on 1997 hardware at speeds up to\n95 cm/s. Its structure is worth internalizing because MPPI keeps one half of it and replaces the\nother:"}]
2e:["$","ul",null,{"children":["\n",["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"Keep:"}]," commands are the decision variable, and the reachable set is a box set by acceleration\nlimits."]}],"\n",["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"Replace:"}]," each candidate is scored along ",["$","em",null,{"children":"one constant-curvature arc"}],", evaluated at its\nendpoint. A hypothesis class of single arcs cannot express \"slow, drift left, then turn hard\nright\" — not badly, but ",["$","em",null,{"children":"at all"}],"."]}],"\n"]}]
